grammar.title: 5A: Past tenses - simple, continuous, perfect
grammar.explanation:
**Past simple** (worked, went, devoured) is for finished actions in the past. We use it when we say, ask, or know when the action happened.

We also use **past simple** for repeated past actions, like the big family **feast** you enjoyed every winter.

**Past continuous** (was/were + verb-ing) shows an action in progress at a specific past time. It often pairs with a short **past simple** action that interrupts it.

We also use **past continuous** with while for two actions happening together. Never use it with non-action verbs like want, need, or know.

**Past perfect** (had + past participle) talks about the earlier of two past actions. It tells us which action finished first.

In stories, the three tenses work as a team. **Past continuous** sets the scene, **past simple** says what happened, and **past perfect** explains what had happened before.
examples: We *were cooking* dinner when the guests arrived. (an action in progress, interrupted)
She *was savoring* her dessert while he *was devouring* his. (two actions at the same time)
They *had eaten* everything when we arrived with the cake. (the earlier of two past actions)
The aroma *was filling* the kitchen when the phone rang. (interrupted action)
I *craved* chocolate all week, so I finally baked a cake. (finished past action)
He *had never tasted* homemade bread before that day. (an experience before a past moment)

practice.q: Which tense sets the scene at the start of a story, as in 'It was raining and we were waiting'?
practice.a: Past continuous — it paints the background, while the main events use the past simple.

practice.q: The train left before I arrived at the station. Which tense describes 'the train left'?
practice.a: Past perfect — 'The train had left before I arrived.' It is the earlier of the two past actions.

practice.q: Can you say 'I was craving chocolate when he called'?
practice.a: No — crave is a non-action verb. Say 'I craved chocolate when he called.'
